content.thinking:
I'm planning whimsical proportions with a big head, chubby body, and smaller legs, then setting up Three.js helpers for merging geometries and fur textures with white tufts and grey tips. Writing creature geometry code...

Defining radius keyframes...

Shifting the whole body up by 0.02 brings the bottom to 0.105 and top to 0.6, matching real capybara shoulder proportions. I'm adjusting the neck and head joint positions and stations to build the skull shape, targeting a head top around 0.6 to align with the back.

Continuing head stations, the muzzle narrows and caps round into a nose pad near 0.7 - I'm keeping it round rather than boxier for a chubby, whimsical look, and the head joint feeds into a skull loft bone.

Now I'm defining the jaw joint and sweeping a tapered capsule for the lower jaw, shrinking width and height along its length to form a rounded chin.

Checking the geometry, the jaw capsule overlaps the muzzle loft somewhat since the jaw center sits inside the head bottom boundary, but the chin still pokes out visibly at the front, which reads fine. I'm positioning small incisor boxes near the mouth line, though the upper lip bottom and jaw top nearly coincide, so I need to make sure the jaw's upper edge reads as below the lip line rather than overlapping it.

I need to resolve the depth conflict between jaw, teeth, and muzzle front: the jaw cap sits around z .62, so teeth placed near .625-.632 would clash. I'll tuck the teeth under the nose pad instead, placing them near the lower front lip around z .69 so the muzzle face visually hides the jaw setback behind it.

I'll use ray-casting from above to find the actual skull surface at the muzzle front, then position the teeth as a small box embedded into that hit point so the top is hidden and the bottom pokes out slightly. For the nose pad, I'll similarly ray-cast to find the tip of the muzzle and offset an ellipsoid backward from that point so it protrudes outward by about .028, then plan small nostril details on either side.

Now I'm working out ear placement using a similar ray-casting approach against the head, picking a direction vector that angles the ear outward and forward, and sizing the ear as a flattened ellipsoid oriented so its length runs upward and its width faces sideways.

Now placing the daisy near the ear, offset slightly so it sits between the ear and the top rather than overlapping the bird's feet. I'll skip adding separate cheek spheres since the loft is wide enough, and just paint blush instead, then set up sleepy eyelids on the eye hits.

For whiskers, I'm casting rays from the muzzle center outward at several azimuth and elevation angles to find hit points, then building each whisker as a curve from the hit point through a control point to a tip, sprouted onto the head bone.

Now I'm moving to leg construction, defining a reusable leg-building function that takes joint positions, names, and parent joint, then using a limb helper to build the hind leg from a hip root point through to the foot.

I'm checking that the hip, knee, and ankle targets stay within the body silhouette and that the three-segment IK chain lengths roughly sum to the total root-to-foot distance, while verifying the knee position falls inside the body outline at that height.

For the front leg I'm setting up a similar two-segment IK chain from shoulder to wrist with a forward bend hint, then tapering the leg radius smoothly along the whole chain so it reads naturally at both the body and paw ends.

Working through the paw geometry now: placing the foot pad ellipsoid at the ankle joint and fanning out individual toe chains from its front edge, with each toe's base and tip positions offset by its index so they splay slightly outward.

For the nails, I'm adding small blunt spikes at each toe tip oriented along the chain's tangent direction, giving capybaras their characteristic hoof-like dark claws rather than sharp points. I'm also setting up the color gradient for the lower legs and feet, darkening toward brownish tones to distinguish the paws from the body fur.

Now I'm tallying the full joint hierarchy: spine, pelvis, neck, head, jaw, ears, four legs with multiple toe joints each (front feet four toes, hind feet three), plus eyelid hinge joints that let the dome-shaped eye covers rotate for blinking, and I'm starting to sketch out a separate bird skeleton with its own body, head, and beak joints.

Writing bird skeleton coordinates...

Still shaping tail feathers...

Now I'm planning the bird body as a scaled sphere part attached to the birdBody bone, with the head positioned above and forward, a beak cone extending from the head's front, and eyes placed on the face. For the wings, I'm setting up joints at the body's sides angled back and down, then shaping the folded wing outline as an extrusion with thickness along the appropriate axis for the left side.

I'll add a slight tilt to the wing and keep the geometry simple for now, planning to verify visually with test renders. Now sketching the wing outline shape with shoulder, tip, and trailing points.

Still writing wing coloring logic...

Now moving on to the bird legs, setting up each as a two-joint chain.

I'll simplify the leg to a single joint with toes parented to it, then move on to the bird's crest spikes, beak coloring (yellow-orange with darker underside), black eyes with white highlights, and a pinkish cheek blush ellipsoid.

Now I'm scattering fur cards across the body, neck, and cheeks with different densities and filters, plus adding chin ruff hair and leg thigh tufts, with a default flow direction angled back and down for body fur.

For coloring the cards, I'm pulling tint from the countershade paint at each card's root position, darkening the tips for depth, and adding a subtle darker dorsal "saddle" tone where the surface normal points upward, layered with mottling for a warm cinnamon capybara palette.

Now I'm filling in the small color palette: peachy belly, blush cheeks, dark plum nose, cream teeth, plus accent colors for the bird, daisy, and ladybug details, along with a darker skin tone for the foot pads. I'm sketching out the head paint function, starting with the base coat and lightening the muzzle area.

I need to import the paint helpers (resolve, mix, mottle, countershade, etc.) from the paint module, and use Vector3 math for hit points since surfaces return Frame-based hits. For placing features like the bird, I'll cast rays from the skull surface downward and handle potential null hits.

For the eye geometry, I'm using a low-segment sphere for simplicity, and designing the lid as a dome-shaped hemisphere whose pole axis tilts outward along the eye's normal direction by about 25 degrees to give it a sleepy, angled look.

The eyelid ring sits as a torus oriented perpendicular to that same tilt axis, and the pupil becomes a large glossy dark sphere embedded slightly into the head surface, with a small white highlight sphere offset toward the front and slightly downward for a glint effect.

For the fur tufts, I'm sketching them as SVG blade shapes—several overlapping pointed paths with gradient fills shifting from white to grey to suggest shading and depth, since gradients render fine when the SVG is rasterized as an image texture.

Now I'm thinking through sizing and placement: a 40x64 viewBox scaled to 128px, with stud cards leaning mostly flat against the surface so they stay visible rather than edge-on. Starting to write the actual builder code—setting up the root structure and a helper function for constructing feet with toe joints.

Working out foot anatomy: each toe is a two-point chain forming a single joint, swept into a rounded shape, with the ankle positioned slightly above the floor and the leg radius determining where the limb meets the pad.

I'm checking that the leg sweep bottoms out right at floor level, with the pad ellipsoid sitting underneath and coated with a gradient paint running from the foot up toward the ankle, then tracing how the limb function returns its joint chain for further use.

I'm setting the chain parenting so front legs attach at the spine joint and hind legs attach at the hips, then considering adding haunch ellipsoids near the rump for extra roundness, coated to match the body. I still need to write the whiskers and figure out how the skull surface loft converts into a sweep, plus confirm the hit-test function returns nullable results that I'll force-unwrap where needed.

For the ladybug, I'm placing its body as a scaled sphere sitting on the detected surface point, adding a small black head sphere and tiny black dot spheres positioned using local ellipsoid coordinates, plus a thin dark center line for the classic look. Writing daisy geometry...

Still writing leaf geometry...

Skipping the hat idea, I'll move on to writing out the complete file now.
